"Remit payment" → pay; "stipulated timeframe" → the date on this notice (and a good notice prints that date in bold nearby — the original buries the one fact that matters); "may result in the assessment of" → will add, since "may" here is a threat pretending to be a possibility. Note the rewrite keeps the conditional structure — if/then — because the consequence genuinely is conditional. Plain language doesn't mean softening the government's leverage; it means the owner should finish the sentence knowing exactly what happens and by when.
Explain the hyphen difference: "a small business owner" versus "a small-business owner," with an example where it matters.

Without the hyphen, "small" most naturally modifies "business" — but it can also read as modifying the owner: a small person who owns a business. "Small-business owner" welds "small-business" into one adjective, so the owner runs a small business regardless of their height. Usually context rescues the unhyphenated version, which is why the rule feels fussy — until it doesn't: "We interviewed a small business owner" in a profile of a 6'4" founder has launched a thousand misreadings and at least a few jokes in print. Compound adjectives before a noun get hyphens when the grouping isn't obvious. After the noun, the hyphen usually drops: "her business is small."
Choose and defend: "From his silence, I ___ that he disagreed." (imply / infer) — and why does the distinction matter in writing?

"Infer." The speaker or writer implies — they put a suggestion into their words or behavior. The listener or reader infers — they draw a conclusion out. His silence contained the implication; you performed the inference. The distinction matters because the two words assign the act to opposite ends of a communication, and swapping them misattributes responsibility: "Are you inferring I'm lying?" accuses the listener of concluding; "Are you implying I'm lying?" accuses the speaker of hinting — in an argument, those are very different charges. Memory hook: the writer implies, the reader infers; implications go in, inferences come out.
A trail guide says: "At the fork, take the path that goes up. The summit is a while after that." Hikers keep getting lost. Rewrite it.

"At the fork (about 20 minutes from the trailhead), take the right-hand path, marked with a blue blaze on a pine tree. The trail climbs steeply for half a mile, then levels at a stone cairn. From the cairn, the summit is another 10 minutes along the ridge. If you reach a stream crossing, you've taken the left fork — go back."

"The path that goes up" fails because both paths go up, eventually — the writer knew which fork they meant and described it by its destination instead of its appearance at the decision point. Good directions describe what the traveler sees when the choice arrives: right hand, blue blaze, a named tree. Add distances and an error check (the stream) and the instruction becomes self-correcting.
A paragraph argues: "Libraries are obsolete. Everyone has the internet now. Besides, maintaining all those buildings is expensive." Strengthen the argument's structure — even if you disagree with it.

Stronger version: "Libraries cost this town $1.2 million a year to maintain. Most of what they once uniquely provided — reference books, newspapers, internet access — now reaches most homes directly. The council should ask what a library offers that a laptop doesn't, and fund only that."

The original asserts ("obsolete") and gestures ("everyone has the internet") — "everyone" is false on its face, and one counterexample (a resident without internet) collapses it. The rewrite does three structural things: quantifies the cost, narrows the claim to what's defensible ("most of what they once uniquely provided"), and ends with a testable demand instead of a verdict. Strengthening an argument you oppose is the best editing exercise there is: it forces structure apart from agreement, and it reveals whether the weakness was the position or just its scaffolding.

This paragraph's sentences are fine individually but the paragraph doesn't flow: "The committee approved the budget. The budget includes funding for road repairs. Road repairs will begin in the spring. The spring schedule depends on the weather." What's the underlying technique that fixes it?

Each sentence should begin where the previous one ended — old information first, new information last, so the sentences chain: "The committee approved the budget, which includes funding for road repairs. The repairs will begin in the spring, weather permitting."

The original actually attempts this (budget → road repairs → spring) but restarts each sentence with a full noun and a dead stop, so the chain clanks instead of flowing. The fix merges the links: the new fact at the end of one sentence ("road repairs") becomes the subject of the next, and the final sentence ends on the genuinely new point (the weather caveat) instead of repeating the chain. When a paragraph feels choppy despite clear sentences, diagram the first and last three words of each — flow lives at the seams.

Rewrite the lead of this announcement, which currently reads: "In accordance with the new policy adopted by the board at its September meeting, and in order to better serve our patrons, the library will be implementing a new system for reserving study rooms, effective next month."

"Starting next month, you'll be able to reserve library study rooms online."

The original spends 38 words on provenance (the board, the September meeting, the policy) before reaching the only thing a patron cares about: what changes, when, and for whom. "In order to better serve our patrons" is the emptiest phrase in institutional writing — no announcement has ever been made in order to serve patrons worse. The rewrite also chooses "you" as the subject, which announcements to the public should do whenever possible: the reader is the protagonist of the change. The policy history isn't deleted from the document — it moves to paragraph two, where the readers who want it (board watchers, journalists) will find it.

An email to a landlord reads: "I am writing to inform you that the heating in my apartment has not been functioning properly for quite some time now, and I would be grateful if you could possibly look into this matter at your earliest convenience." Make it polite but effective.

"I'm writing about the heating in apartment 4B — it has been out since Tuesday, and the apartment is at 58°F. Could someone come by this week? I'm home after 5 p.m. on weekdays, or I can arrange access during the day if you give me a day's notice."

The original is so deferential it dissolves: "not been functioning properly for quite some time" gives the landlord nothing to act on and no sense of urgency, and "at your earliest convenience" formally grants permission to delay. Polite-but-effective runs on specifics: dates, a measured temperature (58°F converts a complaint into a fact), a concrete request (this week), and flexibility about access — which makes saying yes easy. Courtesy is in the tone and the cooperation offered, not in vagueness about what you need.
